title: Psychology on Trial
lead: Classic psychology experiments, in short parts of about ten minutes. In each part your professor Dr Hale opens one case. You take part in it, read the objections, and decide what is left of the result.

how: Each part takes about ten minutes. You open one case with Dr Hale, your professor.
Some choices are your own opinion, with no right or wrong. Some check your reading, and some check how carefully you write. A red ✕ shows a slip and a better sentence.
Tap an underlined word to see what it means. Open "Sources" at the end of each part to see where the facts come from.

words.definition: doing what a person in authority tells you to do
words.example: Our first subject is obedience.

words.definition: a person who offers to take part in something without being forced
words.example: You are a volunteer for a study of memory.

words.definition: accepted as having the right to give orders or make decisions
words.example: Yale is a famous and legitimate institution.

words.definition: a person who secretly works with the researcher while pretending to be an ordinary participant
words.example: In fact he is a confederate: an actor who works for the experimenter.

words.definition: to pause before you do something because you are not sure
words.example: If you hesitate, the experimenter answers with a prod.

words.definition: a short push; here, a standard sentence that tells someone to go on
words.example: The experimenter answers with a prod.

words.definition: strong feelings of worry, pain or unhappiness
words.example: Many volunteers showed clear distress.

words.definition: making someone believe something that is not true
words.example: The whole study relied on deception.

words.definition: a fixed series of actions that are done in a particular order
words.example: Forty men took part in a procedure at Yale.

words.definition: the result of something
words.example: The outcome was far higher than the experts had predicted.

words.definition: to do what you are told or asked to do
words.example: Ordinary people may comply with an authority.

words.definition: worried and upset
words.example: Many volunteers were visibly troubled.

words.definition: good enough to be allowed
words.example: Was the research itself acceptable?

words.definition: to vary between a lowest and a highest value
words.example: The share ranged from 28 to 91 per cent.

words.definition: normal or usual for a kind of thing
words.example: Harm that is more typical of modern life.

words.definition: doubting whether something is true or good
words.example: Be sceptical of the headline and of its critics.

words.definition: the health, safety and happiness of a person or group
words.example: Her main objection was about the volunteers' welfare.

words.definition: a person's agreement to take part after being told honestly what will happen
words.example: They had not given real informed consent.

words.definition: to explain the true purpose of a study to participants after it has finished
words.example: Every volunteer was told the truth in a debrief.

words.definition: a request that speaks to a person's values or feelings
words.example: Appeals to the value of science worked better than orders.

words.definition: a collection of old documents and records
words.example: A third kind of criticism came from the archive.

words.definition: a public argument about something that people strongly disagree about
words.example: Here is a summary of the ethical controversy.

words.definition: an explanation of what something means
words.example: The second objection is about interpretation.

words.definition: a group of people chosen to make decisions or give advice
words.example: Research ethics committees became routine.

words.definition: to make something no longer valid or true
words.example: Neither objection cancels the study.

words.definition: to feel that you share the aims or feelings of a person or group
words.example: The volunteers identified with the scientific cause.

words.definition: to perform or organise something again
words.example: They restaged the procedure for a film.

words.definition: complicated and not clear or tidy
words.example: The archive tells a messier story.

words.definition: a version of a procedure in which one thing is changed
words.example: Milgram ran about twenty variations of the study.

words.definition: a rule or measure that protects people from harm
words.example: Stopping at 150 volts was a reasonable safeguard.

words.definition: statistically significant: unlikely to be caused by chance alone
words.example: The difference was not statistically significant.

words.definition: a new study that repeats an earlier study to check its result
words.example: This is a partial replication.

words.definition: a warning that a statement is only true under certain conditions
words.example: Every claim needs a caveat.

words.definition: a statement that something is true, especially one that is not yet proved
words.example: Let us test some claims.

words.definition: strong and not easily broken or disproved
words.example: The finding appears robust in a limited sense.

words.definition: to say that something is true for a whole group or for all situations
words.example: The finding cannot be generalised without caution.

words.definition: belonging to the present time
words.example: The result is contemporary as well as historical.

words.definition: to stay in the same state or place
words.example: Three things seem to remain.

words.definition: to get the same result again by repeating a study
words.example: Can the result be reproduced?

words.definition: connected with what is morally right
words.example: Researchers now use ethical designs.

words.definition: an opinion or decision about something, especially after thinking carefully
words.example: You answered a study of visual judgement.

words.definition: one attempt or round of a test
words.example: Each card is a new trial.

words.definition: most of the people in a group
words.example: The actors formed a majority.

words.definition: agreed by everybody, with no exception
words.example: On twelve cards the actors were unanimous.

words.definition: to give way to pressure and do what others want
words.example: Three quarters of the volunteers yielded to the group at least once.

words.definition: changing what you say or do to match a group
words.example: The subject of this case is conformity.

words.definition: a nervous, uncomfortable feeling when something is uncertain or stressful
words.example: Many volunteers showed tension.

words.definition: to change something so that it is no longer true or accurate
words.example: Group pressure can distort judgement.

words.definition: not clear, because it can be understood in more than one way
words.example: Sherif used an ambiguous task.

words.definition: a guess about a size, amount or value
words.example: Their estimates moved towards the group's.

words.definition: easy to see or understand
words.example: The answer is obvious.

words.definition: the ability to think and act without being controlled by others
words.example: The word independence comes first in the title.

words.definition: to understand something in the wrong way
words.example: Asch's work was misinterpreted over the years.

words.definition: a book that teaches a subject at school or university
words.example: Griggs checked twenty recent textbooks.

words.definition: without your name or identity being known
words.example: They answered anonymously in separate booths.

words.definition: fair, giving the right weight to all sides
words.example: Which version reports the result in the most balanced way?

words.definition: a small closed space for one person, for example for voting or for a test
words.example: They answered in separate booths.

words.definition: choosing only some things and leaving others out
words.example: Selective reporting gives more space to one half of the result.

words.definition: importance or influence given to something
words.example: The two numbers were not given the same weight.

words.definition: a university student who is studying for a first degree
words.example: They tested Japanese undergraduates.

words.definition: a person who supports you, especially against opposition
words.example: The volunteer had an ally.

words.definition: to stop rising or falling and stay at about the same level
words.example: The pull rose to 31.8 per cent and then levelled off.

words.definition: a small group chosen to represent a larger group
words.example: The sample of studies was uneven.

words.definition: a study that combines the results of many earlier studies
words.example: Bond and Smith published a meta-analysis of 133 studies.

words.definition: valuing the group and its harmony more than the individual
words.example: In more collectivist countries conformity was higher.

words.definition: to become smaller, weaker or less
words.example: In the United States, conformity had declined since the 1950s.

words.definition: the main point of a story, put in a short form
words.example: The textbook headline is simpler than the evidence.

words.definition: a fixed, simple idea about a group of people
words.example: Later work has not confirmed the stereotype.

words.definition: to use power or influence to affect something
words.example: Do online groups exert the same pressure?

words.definition: the act of accepting the power or control of another person
words.example: Obedience may be less about blind submission than about identification with a cause.

words.definition: a weakness or a point beyond which something cannot be trusted or used
words.example: Both studies have clear limitations.

words.definition: an idea about the reason for something that has not yet been proved
words.example: A hypothesis about the reasons is still being tested.

words.definition: used to compare two facts and show that they are different
words.example: Case 1 studied an authority, whereas Case 2 studied a group.

words.definition: in the same way
words.example: Similarly, both studies used deception.

words.definition: used to show a clear difference between two things
words.example: In contrast to Case 1, Case 2 produced more independent answers.

words.definition: a habit or a likely way of behaving
words.example: Why might a tendency to follow the group exist at all?

words.definition: a feature that helps a living thing to survive in its environment
words.example: Researchers treat it as a possible adaptation.

","^Conclusion. After more than sixty years, three things seem to ‹remain›. A situation can move many people further than they expect. ","^Further research. In 2017, Dariusz Doliński and his colleagues repeated the procedure with 80 adults in Poland, again stopping at 150 volts: 90 per cent went to the highest level that was offered. Over the decades, Blass's review had found no significant trend in obedience rates, so the question is no longer whether the result can be ‹reproduced=reproduce›. ","^Conclusion. A classic study is a starting point, not a verdict. Read side by side, the two cases share a pattern: a strong headline, a larger and quieter second half of the result, and a ‹hypothesis› about the reasons that is still being tested. The best summary of each case names its numbers, its limits and its critics. ","#","^card: Conclusion and further research","/#","
","^Further research. Haslam and Reicher (2012) compared Milgram's studies with another famous study of roles and power, and argued that in both people followed leaders they identified with, rather than simply obeying. Cialdini and Goldstein (2004) reviewed the wider research on compliance and conformity in everyday life. A different line of work asks why a collective tendency exists at all: evolutionary researchers treat copying the majority as a possible adaptation. Boyd and Richerson (1985) modelled when it pays to copy the majority, Haun, Rekers and Tomasello (2012) found majority-biased copying in chimpanzees and in two-year-old children, and Claidière and Whiten (2012) reviewed conformity in animals and humans. These are hypotheses about origins, not proof that Asch's volunteers were acting on an ancient instinct. A useful habit for any student of psychology follows from all of this: before you use a famous number, find out what it left out. ","#","^card: Conclusion and further research","/#","
